subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Ultimatum Game
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Ultimatum Game.

hook.text: I offer to split $10. I keep $9, you get $1. Take it or we both get nothing. Most people reject the deal.

buildup.text: Rationally you should accept any amount over zero. A dollar is better than nothing. But fairness overrides logic.

discovery.text: The ultimatum game reveals that humans will pay a cost to punish unfairness—even when it hurts them.

twist.text: Brain scans show the anterior insula lights up on unfair offers—the same region activated by disgust.

climax.text: Cross-cultural studies show variation, but every society rejects extremely unfair splits. Fairness is universal.

punchline.text: We'd rather have nothing than accept injustice.

quiz.question: What do most people do with a very unfair offer in the ultimatum game?
options: Reject it, even at personal cost

details.summary: In the ultimatum game, one player proposes a split of money and the other accepts or rejects it. Rational self-interest predicts accepting any offer above zero, but people routinely reject low offers to punish unfairness, even at personal cost.
details.whyItMatters: The ultimatum game shows that humans are not purely rational maximizers. Fairness, social norms, and punishment of cheaters play central roles in economic decisions.
takeaways: People reject unfair offers even when losing money
Offers below 20-30 percent are typically rejected
Fairness enforcement is a universal but culturally variable norm

faq.question: Why do people reject low ultimatum offers?
faq.answer: Rejecting a low offer punishes unfairness and enforces social norms of equity. Brain imaging shows that unfair offers activate anger-related regions. People are willing to pay a cost to signal that exploitative behavior is unacceptable, which benefits cooperation in the long run.

faq.question: Do ultimatum game results vary across cultures?
faq.answer: Yes. While all cultures show some rejection of low offers, the threshold varies. Some indigenous groups offer more than half. Industrialized societies tend to converge around 40-50 percent offers. Cultural norms about fairness, reciprocity, and economic exchange shape the specific patterns.
